Social media guidelines are instructions and recommendations for how employees, partners, and collaborators should represent a brand on social media.
While employees are the primary audience, they’re just as useful for agencies, contractors, and influencers who speak on your brand’s behalf.
Think of social media guidelines as your brand’s manual for social media best practices. They should outline how to behave on social media in a way that’s positive and safe.
Social media guidelines are not the same as a social media policy or a style guide. More on how those three documents differ in the next section.

That said, keeping all three documents together makes them far easier to use (and actually follow). Want to learn more? Take Hootsuite Academy’s free course Implementing social media governance within your organization.

What’s the difference between social media guidelines, a social media policy, and a style guide?
The short version: guidelines recommend, policies require, and style guides standardize. All three serve different purposes, and most organizations need all three.
Here’s how they compare side by side:
Recommends how to behave on social media
All employees, with HR and legal weight behind it
Annually, or when platforms and regulations change
When brand assets or messaging change
If you only have budget and bandwidth for one document, start with guidelines. They’re the most useful to the most people, and they give you a foundation to build a formal policy on later.
Why do social media guidelines matter?
Social media guidelines matter because they protect your brand, ensure compliance with regulations, and empower employees to participate online with confidence.
Here are the biggest benefits of social media guidelines:
How do social media guidelines protect your brand?
Clear social media guidelines help protect your brand from risk, especially when they work alongside a solid social media policy.

They cover how everyday social activity connects back to brand reputation and even compliance. From the basics to the high-stakes stuff, good guidelines make it clear that what employees do on social media really does reflect on the brand.

These risks are real. A single post that shares confidential information, misstates a product claim, or skips a required disclosure can trigger a legal review, a regulatory complaint, or unwanted media attention. Guidelines won’t prevent every mistake, but they remove the most common excuse: “I didn’t know.”
How do guidelines keep employees aligned with regulations?
Social media regulations don’t just apply to official brand accounts. They apply to employees, too.
This is obvious in heavily regulated industries like healthcare and finance, but it matters just as much for retail, service, and consumer brands.

For example, the Federal Trade Commission’s social media disclosure guidelines require people to clearly disclose when they’re being paid, gifted products, or otherwise compensated for endorsements. That includes employees, influencers, and partners.

Rules also change. Platform policies, the EU Digital Services Act, and state-level social media laws all shift on their own timelines, which is a good argument for reviewing your guidelines on a set schedule, informed by current social media trends, rather than only when something goes wrong.

To avoid confusion (and costly mistakes), include any relevant regulations directly in your social media guidelines. It’s a good idea to also add specific examples that make the requirements easy for everyone to understand.
How do guidelines encourage brand advocacy?
Every employee is a potential brand ambassador, but not everyone knows exactly what’s okay to share on their own social media.

That’s where social media guidelines come in. They give your team clear guardrails to talk about their work in a way that’s positive, inclusive, and on brand. When people know the rules, they feel more comfortable hyping up your brand (and their work).

It takes the stress out of posting and helps everyone show up confidently online without second-guessing.

What should a social media guidelines document include?
At minimum, a strong social media guidelines document should explain who the guidelines apply to, what types of social media activity they cover, and how employees are expected to act online.
It can also include practical guardrails around privacy, copyright, cybersecurity, accessibility, AI use, and disclosure.

What are the 5 W’s your guidelines should cover?
Strong social media guidelines start with the basics: who, what, when, where, and why. Covering these upfront ensures everyone is on the same page:
The 5 W’s of social media guidelines
Who: Clearly state who the guidelines apply to. This is anyone who works with your company, including employees, contractors, agency partners, students, or influencers. Be specific.

What: Clarify what counts as company-related social media use. This typically includes posts from official social media accounts, work-related content shared from personal social media accounts, and sometimes personal social media use during work hours or on company devices.
When: Add a “last updated” date so people know which version is current and when changes take effect.

Where: Define what you mean by “social media.” This could include a list of social media channels, official accounts, and branded hashtags. Or, it could be a broader definition that includes platforms like Reddit and Quora.

Why: Explain why the guidelines exist in the first place. People are much more likely to follow the rules when they understand how they protect both employees and the brand. Touch on any specific compliance requirements that apply to your industry (like HIPAA or FINRA).
What high-level dos and don’ts should you include?
In an ideal world, every employee would read every line of your social media policy and guidelines. In reality, most won’t.
That’s why it helps to lead with a quick, punchy list of basic expectations. Think of this as your social media code of conduct at a glance.
Don’t go into too much detail here, since you’ll do that in later sections. Here’s a sample list you can copy and paste or tweak for your specific needs:
DO mention the company as your employer in your social media bio (if you talk about company matters)
DON’T engage with competitors or customers in an inappropriate way
DO share company social media posts, events, and stories
DON’T share company secrets or confidential information about your colleagues or customers
DO express your own opinion, just make sure it’s clear you’re not speaking on behalf of the company
DON’T comment on legal matters pertaining to the company
DO report harassment you’ve experienced or noticed
DON’T engage with trolls or negative comments
DO disclose when content was created or edited with AI tools
DON’T use AI to generate content that impersonates real people or fabricates endorsements
Employees should always be clear about when they’re speaking for themselves versus on behalf of your company.

Adding a disclosure to their social profile or bio is a good start. Something like “All opinions expressed are my own” makes it clear that these are not official viewpoints, but personal views, like this university strategist and instructor does here.

However, when employees post about company-related topics, disclosure isn’t optional. The FTC’s Endorsement Guides require them to identify themselves as employees in the post itself, not just in their bio. That’s a rule, not a suggestion.

To make this easy (and consistent), work with your legal or compliance team to approve a few clear, copy-and-paste disclosures. Including those directly in your social media guidelines helps employees get it right without guessing.
Remind your team that confidential company information is confidential off the clock, too. Some of the biggest no-nos for sharing on social are:
Upcoming products that haven’t been officially announced

Clarify that privacy and confidentiality should be respected across all social media platforms. That also includes photos taken at your workplace or workplace events. These can be especially challenging for organizations subject to HIPAA or FERPA.
It’s also good practice to remind employees to review their social media profile settings to make sure their personal information remains protected.
Include a reminder in your social media posting guidelines to respect ownership from:
When in doubt, the rule of thumb is relatively simple: if it’s not yours, and you don’t have permission, don’t post it. (Except through native resharing functions.)
AI-generated images and text raise additional copyright questions that courts and regulators are still working through. When in doubt, have your legal team weigh in before posting.

Your employees may already be vigilant about phishing scams and the like. Still, it never hurts to review cyber-safety basics, especially if you collect information about customers or clients.

According to the FTC, social media was the second most common way fraudsters contacted victims in 2025 when measured by the volume of reports involving a loss, accounting for 28% of those reports, behind websites or apps at 31%. The FTC also flagged social media as the costliest contact method by total dollars lost. Either way, employee accounts sit squarely in the risk zone, which is why cybersecurity deserves a clear spot in your social media guidelines.
We’ve got a whole post on social media security that can help you craft your social media guidelines on this front.
Here’s a quick refresh of smart cybersecurity habits:
Only activate geolocation services on apps when necessary
Use a different password for every social account
Never share passwords with others. Create separate access credentials for all team members who access corporate accounts
Use two-factor (or multi-factor) authentication to login to social networks
Limit the personal and professional information you share, and avoid online “quizzes” that fish for password hints
Use personal credentials for personal accounts (rather than your corporate email)
Make sure your internet connection is secure, and be cautious on public Wi-Fi networks
Do not download or click on suspicious content
It’s important for every employer and brand to promote accessibility and inclusivity on and off social media. It also helps employees feel supported.
Here are some common accessibility and inclusivity guidelines for social media:
Add alt text to images and captions or subtitles to videos
Be thoughtful about representation in social media imagery. This includes stock imagery, emojis, and branded visuals.
Don’t make assumptions about gender, race, experience, or ability
Avoid gender- or race-specific emojis when they aren’t necessary
Feel free to share your preferred pronouns (and always respect the pronouns of others)
Use title case for hashtags (this makes them more legible for screen readers)
Report and remove any comments that are sexist, racist, ableist, ageist, homophobic, or hateful to any group or person from your owned social channels
Consider how content may be perceived by different segments of your target audience
Use AI-assisted alt text and auto-captions as a starting point, then review and edit them before publishing. Automated tools often miss names, context, and technical terms.
Take advantage of platform-native accessibility features, like Instagram’s custom alt text field and LinkedIn’s closed captioning upload

Your guidelines should clearly define how employees (and your social media team) are expected to handle trolls, harassment, or negative comments. Should they ignore or escalate? And when is it okay to respond directly?
For example, it may be appropriate to acknowledge a concern publicly, then move the conversation to direct messages for resolution.

Anyone who manages comments on your owned channels should also have a clear content moderation policy to lean on. It should cover when to hide, delete, or respond to comments, and who needs to be looped in for sensitive situations. You can link to that policy here if needed.
Finally, make sure everyone knows how to report issues they come across. If support is needed, be explicit about where to go and who to contact.
Providing protocol and tools helps your team nip problems in the bud before they grow into a full-blown social media crisis.

Most teams are already using AI to draft captions, resize creative, or summarize comments. Your guidelines should say what’s allowed, what needs review, and what’s off limits, so people aren’t guessing.
Here’s what to cover in your AI-generated content section:
Approved tools: List the AI tools employees can use for work-related content, and note which ones are not approved for handling customer or confidential data

Disclosure expectations: Spell out when AI involvement needs to be disclosed in the post itself, especially for synthetic imagery, voice, or video. Several platforms now require AI labels on realistic synthetic media, so check each network’s current rules
Human review: Require a person to review and fact-check AI-generated copy before it publishes. AI tools confidently invent statistics, product details, and quotes
Customer responses: Clarify whether AI can draft replies to customers, who approves them, and which topics always need a human (complaints, health or financial questions, legal matters)
Likeness and impersonation: Prohibit using AI to recreate the voice or appearance of real people, including employees, customers, and competitors, without written consent
Data input limits: State clearly that confidential company information, unreleased product details, and customer data should never be pasted into public AI tools
Expectations shift from platform to platform, and your guidelines should acknowledge that. A LinkedIn comment and a TikTok duet carry different risks and different norms.
You don’t need an exhaustive section for every network. A short list of considerations per major platform is usually enough:
LinkedIn: The most common place employees discuss work. Clarify how to describe their role, what company information is fair game, and whether they should tag the company page
Instagram: Heavy on visuals, so copyright and likeness rules matter most here. Cover photo consent for workplace images and alt text requirements
TikTok: More creative freedom, more risk of context collapse. Note expectations around trending audio licensing, filming on company property, and disclosing employment in the video or caption
X: Fast-moving and public. Set expectations around replying to critics, quote-posting competitors, and when to escalate instead of engage
Reddit and community forums: Users are highly sensitive to undisclosed promotion. Require employees to disclose their affiliation before discussing company products
Threads, Bluesky, and emerging platforms: Note that guidelines apply to any public social platform, including new ones, so you don’t need to rewrite the document every time a network launches

Your social media guidelines shouldn’t live in a vacuum. Link out to related resources like your social media policy, style guide, and community guidelines so people can easily find deeper detail when they need it.
You may also want to include links to broader brand documents, like your brand identity guidelines or employee handbook.

If you offer social media training or resources, include those as well. And don’t forget your employee advocacy program. Giving staff access to pre-approved content makes it easier (and safer) for them to share and participate.
How to write social media guidelines step by step
Writing social media guidelines takes less time than most teams expect, as long as you line up the right stakeholders early. Here’s the process in eight steps:
How to write social media guidelines in 8 steps
Send it for legal and HR review

Start by collecting every document that touches social media at your organization. That might include an employee handbook section, a brand style guide, a crisis comms plan, or an old policy nobody has opened since 2019.
Note what’s current, what’s contradictory, and what’s missing. You’ll often find you’re not starting from zero.
Social media guidelines touch legal, HR, communications, IT security, and the social team. Bring them in before you draft, not after.

Ask each group one question: what’s the risk you worry about most? Legal will flag disclosure and copyright. HR will raise harassment and personal account boundaries. IT will want account security rules. Those answers become your section list.
Decide who the guidelines apply to and what counts as company-related activity. This is where the 5 W’s framework earns its keep.
Be specific about personal accounts. Vague scope language is the most common reason guidelines get ignored or challenged.
Work through the sections outlined earlier: dos and don’ts, disclosure, privacy, copyright, cybersecurity, accessibility, negativity, AI use, and channel-specific notes.
Write in plain language. If a sentence needs a legal degree to parse, rewrite it. The goal is a document people actually read, not one that only satisfies a compliance checkbox.
Abstract rules are easy to misinterpret. Concrete examples are not.
For every rule that could be read two ways, show a compliant post and a non-compliant one. Copy-and-paste disclosure language is especially useful here, since it removes the judgment call entirely.
6. Send it for legal and HR review

Your legal team needs to confirm the regulatory language is accurate for your industry and jurisdictions. HR needs to confirm the enforcement language aligns with existing employment agreements and labor law.
Build in two weeks for this step. It almost always takes longer than planned, particularly in regulated industries where errors carry real legal and financial consequences.
Put the final document somewhere people can find it without asking: your intranet, your onboarding packet, your HR portal. Then announce it, rather than quietly uploading it.
Pair the announcement with a short walkthrough. A 20-minute session covering the top five things employees need to know will do more than a 15-page PDF ever will.
Set a recurring annual review before you close the project. Add a trigger-based review too, so platform policy changes, new regulations, or a social media incident prompt an off-cycle update.
Log the “last updated” date on the document itself so nobody is working from a stale version.

To get a sense of the different kinds of social media guidelines out there, we’ve divided these real-world examples by industry.

Like many other post-secondary institutions, the University of Northern Georgia notes that its social media guidelines apply to both employees and students. This helps protect the university’s brand by setting expectations for behavior across the board.

McGill University gets into finer detail, organizing its guidance around a set of general principles that cover accuracy, respect, inclusiveness, privacy, accessibility, and brand identity. (McGill may restructure this page, so check the current version before citing it.)
The social media guidelines for the Ontario Public Service are broken down into four different use categories. They include common-sense guiding principles backed by this important caveat:
“Even if you use disclaimers like ‘the opinions expressed are my own,’ you are still responsible for what you say. What you say publicly may impact you professionally.”

Horizon Health Network is a great reminder that social media guidelines don’t need to be long to be effective. Their guidelines fit on a single page, but still cover reputation, professionalism, and personal use of social media.

One standout line says it all: “If you do identify your affiliation to Horizon (on any social platform) make sure your activities are consistent with the high standards of your profession and Horizon.”
Providence Health & Services combines its official-use social media policy with its social media guidelines for personal use.

“It’s important to remember that you can be held personally and legally responsible for the publicly made opinions and comments you make, even on personally maintained sites and pages … You are required to maintain patient privacy by following Providence Privacy and Security policies and standards and HIPAA rules at all times.”

Chanel offers a masterclass in disclosure. Their guidelines get very specific about sponsored content, calling out exactly what doesn’t count as proper disclosure: “#gifted, #freeproduct, #comped, or #hosted are insufficient as they do not explain who provided the gift or that certain product was free (the FTC does not believe any of these are specific enough).”

Intel’s social media guidelines are one of the longest-running public examples, and they’re worth studying for how plainly they’re written. The document is organized around a short set of rules rather than dense legal language.
The line that gets quoted most often: “If it gives you pause, pause rather than publish.” It’s a useful default for employees facing a judgment call with no obvious answer.
Intel also asks employees to add a disclosure when they write about company-related topics, and to correct mistakes openly rather than quietly deleting posts.

The American Red Cross operates a large volunteer network, which makes scope definition unusually important. Its social media guidance applies to employees and volunteers alike, and it’s written for people who may be posting from the field during an active emergency.
The emphasis is on accuracy and escalation: don’t speculate about an unfolding disaster, don’t share details about people receiving aid, and route anything sensitive to the communications team.
Financial services firms operate under FINRA and SEC rules that treat social media posts as business communications, which means recordkeeping and pre-approval requirements apply.

Vanguard’s public social media guidance reflects that reality. It states clearly that comments on its channels may be reviewed and retained, that it won’t discuss individual account details on social media, and that it does not endorse third-party content shared in its comment sections.
How to roll out and enforce social media guidelines
A finished document does nothing on its own. Rollout is where most guidelines projects quietly fail, usually because the file gets uploaded to a shared drive and never mentioned again.
Announce it properly: Send a company-wide note from a leader, not a buried HR email. Explain what changed and why it protects employees, not just the brand
Run a short training session: Twenty minutes covering the five things people most need to know beats a document nobody opens. Record it for new hires
Build it into onboarding: Add the guidelines to your new-hire packet and ask for acknowledgment, the same way you would for any workplace policy
Make it findable in under 30 seconds: Intranet homepage, HR portal, bookmarked in your team’s shared channel. If someone has to ask where it lives, it’s too hidden
Name the escalation contacts: List real people and channels for reporting harassment, flagging a risky post, or asking a gray-area question
Enforce consistently: Work with HR to define what happens after a violation, and apply it the same way at every level of the organization. Inconsistent enforcement undermines the whole document
Make compliance the easy path: Give employees pre-approved content they can share in a couple of taps. Most violations come from guesswork, not bad intent
Review and update on schedule: Set an annual review and update cycle, plus trigger-based reviews when platform policies or regulations change

What are social media guidelines and why do companies need them?

Social media guidelines explain how employees and partners should represent a brand online, and companies need them to empower their people to post safely. They set clear expectations for behavior, compliance, and disclosure, helping brands avoid legal issues, reputational damage, and awkward social moments.
How do you create social media guidelines for employees?

You create social media guidelines by auditing what you already have, assembling stakeholders from legal, HR, and comms, defining scope, drafting the core sections, and getting legal review before you publish. The step-by-step section above walks through all eight stages, including how to set a review cadence.
What is the difference between social media guidelines and a social media policy?

Social media guidelines are recommendations for how employees should behave on social media, while a social media policy is a formal, enforceable document that outlines rules and consequences. Guidelines are usually owned by marketing or communications; policies are owned by legal or HR and tied to your disciplinary process.
Should social media guidelines address AI-generated content?

Yes, social media guidelines in 2026 should include clear rules about when and how employees can use AI tools to create or edit social media content. Cover approved tools, disclosure requirements for synthetic media, mandatory human review, and a prohibition on pasting confidential data into public AI tools.
How often should you update social media guidelines?

Social media guidelines should be reviewed and updated at least once a year, or whenever there are significant changes to platform policies, regulations, or your organization’s social strategy. Add a “last updated” date to the document so employees always know which version is current.
Do social media guidelines apply to employees’ personal accounts?

Social media guidelines can apply to employees’ personal accounts when their posts reference the company, its products, or its clients, though the scope should be clearly defined in the document. Vague scope language is the most common reason guidelines get ignored or challenged, so be specific about what counts as company-related activity.
What is the etiquette of social media in a professional context?

Social media etiquette in a professional context means being transparent about your affiliation, respecting confidentiality, giving credit to original creators, and engaging respectfully with others online. It also means knowing when to step away, particularly with trolls or escalating comment threads.
What are social media guideline best practices for enterprise organizations?

For enterprise brands, best practices include keeping guidelines simple, scalable, and easy to reference. That means setting clear guardrails, aligning with legal and HR teams, and using tools like Hootsuite Amplify to give employees access to pre-approved content to share online.
What should be included in corporate social media guidelines?

Corporate social media guidelines should cover disclosure and transparency, privacy and confidentiality, copyright, cybersecurity basics, accessibility and inclusion, AI and generative AI use, channel-specific expectations, and how to respond to negative interactions. They should also link out to related policies and resources.
What are examples of effective social media guidelines?

Examples of effective social media guidelines include McGill University, Ontario Public Service, Horizon Health Network, Chanel, Intel, Nordstrom, the American Red Cross, and Vanguard. The common thread: clear expectations, real examples, and common-sense guidance people can actually follow.
